summary:
Kano State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, reaches visitors as well as residents, and provides no legal protection for LGBT+ people. Operating over that national layer, Kano State runs its own religious penal code, the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, which took effect on 26 November 2000.

The statutory ceiling in Kano is the harshest a trans visitor can face anywhere in the country. Under the Kano code, consensual same-sex activity draws 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment where the offender is unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) where the offender is or has been married. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression and sex characteristics in Nigeria (June 2025) lists the same two-tier maximum and records that the capital maximum applies to same-sex acts between women as well as between men.

Gender expression is separately criminalised. Kano's Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law criminalises cross-dressing by men, so presentation that does not match the sex recorded in a visitor's documents carries its own exposure independent of the national statute.

Enforcement machinery is active and visible. The USCIRF 2019 study of Sharia criminal-law implementation draws on 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara and records Hisbah (religious police) activity in each state, with Kano the most active command. In 2023 eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on hisbah premises in Kano state.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. The Home Office note records the Sharia codes across the twelve northern states as remaining in force, with Kano's code on the file as a current instrument rather than a historical one.
tangentialFactors:
Kano's maximum is the extreme point of a comparative pattern inside Nigeria. The Home Office comparative table lists the Kano Sharia Penal Code (2000) as prescribing death by stoning for married or previously married men and 100 lashes with imprisonment of up to one year for unmarried men. It lists Kano and Katsina as carrying a maximum penalty of death for 'lesbianism', while the other ten Sharia states punish the same conduct by flogging and up to six months' imprisonment.

Judicial and religious-police activity is documented rather than theoretical. USCIRF's 2019 sample of 173 Sharia-court cases drawn from 2017 covers Kano alongside Sokoto and Zamfara, and identifies Hisbah presence in all three, with the Kano command the most active of them. Public corporal punishment has been carried out on that machinery: the 2023 flogging of eight people for wearing female clothing at a wedding took place on hisbah premises in Kano state.

The national layer beneath Kano's code supplies the offences most likely to reach a visitor in practice, since the 2014 statute's penalties of 10 to 14 years cover cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, and police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. Kano's stoning maximum sits on top of that baseline rather than replacing it.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kano State are subject to both the national statute and the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, in force since 26 November 2000. The national law criminalises same-sex conduct with penalties of up to 14 years and, per Human Rights Watch, extends to cohabitation between same-sex partners, public display of a same-sex relationship and gay organisational activity, with police using it to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

The Kano code prescribes 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment for unmarried persons convicted of consensual same-sex activity and stoning to death where the offender is or has been married. The Home Office note records this capital maximum as applying to acts between women as well as between men, and records the Kato code alongside Katsina as the two states setting death as the maximum for 'lesbianism'.

The separate Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law criminalises cross-dressing by men, adding a locally enforceable offence for gender non-conforming presentation. Hisbah, the state religious police, carries out enforcement; USCIRF records it as the most active of the Sharia-state commands studied. In 2023 eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on hisbah premises in Kano state.

Nigeria offers no legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the 2014 statute reinforced colonial-era criminalisation rather than removing it.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records whether the Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law has been applied to foreign nationals, or under which section a visitor would be charged for cross-dressing. That application is unresolved on the available material.

The sources do not state how Kano authorities establish the marital-status element on which the stoning maximum turns, nor whether rajm has been carried out for same-sex conduct in Kano. Only the statutory maximum is sourced here.

No sourced account in this inventory covers whether the 2023 public flogging in Kano state led to criminal proceedings against those convicted, or whether the hisbah activity recorded by USCIRF resulted in Sharia-court sentences for same-sex conduct specifically. The USCIRF sample is drawn from 2017 case files and does not disaggregate offences by type in the material available.

Whether Nigeria's reported proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted remains unsettled by these sources; only the Kano-level cross-dressing offence is documented here.

No source addresses how Kano's authorities treat a visitor whose passport gender marker differs from their presentation, or whether entry screening at Kano involves any gender-congruence check. That is not sourced rather than confirmed absent.
